title: A Topological Sorting Criterion for Random Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs
claim: Sortability by a simple graph statistic is high only within a narrow density range and drops sharply elsewhere, across graph families.
layout: 2 side-by-side heatmap panels, shared axes, a colorbar beside each
description: Two side-by-side heatmaps show how well sorting by the number of relatives recovers the causal order, called sortability. Panel (a) covers Erdős–Rényi DAGs and panel (b) covers scale-free DAGs. The x-axis is the number of nodes n, from 2 to about 100. The y-axis is the density parameter c, from 0.5 to 50. Each plot is a triangle, because feasible density grows with n. A viridis colorbar runs from 0.5 (dark purple) to 1.0 (yellow). A bright yellow-green band sits at low density, around c of 2 to 7. Above it the color fades to dark purple, which is near chance. The eye goes first to the bright band along the bottom, then to the dark upper triangle. Each panel has a letter caption beneath it.
caption: Rel-sortability of random ER and SF DAGs with $n$ nodes and density parameter $c$.
abstract: Random directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) based on imposing an order on ErdÅs-RÃ©nyi or scale-free graphs are widely used to generate synthetic data from causal models, in particular for evaluating causal discovery algorithms. We show that the set of nodes reachable via open paths, termed relatives, never decreases along the causal order in all DAGs. We find that it tends to increase strictly for DAGs with certain density parameters, and demonstrate that this pattern can be exploited for causal discovery via sorting by the estimated number of relatives. We note that many simulations in the literature are focused on a narrow range of parameter settings where sorting by relatives yields an excellent proxy for the causal order, and show that a strict increase of relatives leads to a singleton Markov equivalence class. We propose sampling time-series DAGs as a possible alternative and discuss implications for causal discovery and synthetic data generation. Implementations of our algorithms can be found at https://causaldisco.github.io/CausalDisco/.
